desc:
The array nums is a mountain: strictly increasing up to a peak (neither the first nor the last element), then strictly decreasing. The same value can occur once on each slope.

Return the k-th smallest element when all elements are sorted in non-decreasing order (counting duplicates, 1-based). Do it without sorting or merging the whole array: aim for O(log n * log V) where V is the value range.

For example, for nums = [1, 4, 6, 5, 4, 2] the sorted order is 1, 2, 4, 4, 5, 6, so k = 4 gives 4 and k = 5 gives 5.
constraints: nums is guaranteed to be a mountain array
hints: Sorting works in O(n log n). Think about binary searching the value instead: how many elements are ≤ x for a given x?
The answer is the smallest value x for which at least k elements are ≤ x. The count never decreases as x grows.

Count elements ≤ x in O(log n): after locating the peak, the ascending part contributes a prefix (binary search the first value > x) and the descending part contributes a suffix (binary search the first value ≤ x). Binary search x between the smaller end of the array and the peak value.
editorial: Define count(x) = the number of elements ≤ x. It is non-decreasing in x, and the k-th smallest element is the smallest x with count(x) ≥ k; that x is necessarily an element of the array, because the count only jumps at array values.

Computing count(x) uses the mountain structure. Find the peak once. On the ascending part nums[0..peak] the elements ≤ x form a prefix, whose length is the first index with value > x. On the descending part the elements ≤ x form a suffix, which starts at the first index with value ≤ x. The sum of both lengths is count(x).

Binary search x over [min(nums[0], nums[n - 1]), nums[peak]], which takes about 31 rounds for 32-bit values. Each round costs two binary searches of O(log n), so the total is O(log n * log V) time and O(1) space. Merging the two slopes explicitly would take O(n).
